title: The Uneven Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Entrepreneurial Performance: Evidence from a Field Experiment in Kenya
pub: Management Science (published online ahead of print); earlier as HBS Working Paper 24-042 and SSRN 4671369
author: Nicholas G. Otis · Rowan Clarke · Solène Delecourt · David Holtz · Rembrand Koning

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The supplied evidence describes intervention delivery, access control and attrition, but reports no productivity, quality, learning, verification or interaction-cost outcomes. It therefore cannot establish whether AI saved or consumed time, although its controlled design could support such an assessment elsewhere in the source.
qs: The difference in attrition across conditions is 1.2 pp (p = 0.35).

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source excerpt concerns retail advice on adding milk-based snacks and desserts. It does not address legal AI, multidisciplinary implementation, verification, task-specific evaluation, service delivery or lawyer replacement, so its position on the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Assisted performance: Gains vary by skill measure
st.an: The source directly reinforces the cluster’s claim that AI-assisted gains are heterogeneous rather than uniform: average entrepreneurial performance effects are insignificant while initially stronger and weaker entrepreneurs experience materially different effects. It also strengthens the cluster’s robustness caution by showing that this differential weakens under a log-like outcome transformation.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster’s proposition with randomized field evidence outside legal practice: gains on controlled, bounded tasks did not generalize uniformly to open-ended decisions, and outcomes depended on users’ judgment and complementary capabilities. It also reinforces the case for real-world socio-technical evaluation rather than inferring impact from benchmarks or task experiments alone.
qs: Sub-sample analysis shows that the AI assistant caused a 15% increase in per- formance, for high performers but that for low performers, the treatment effect led to an 8% decline in performance relative to the control group.

This increase in performance        inequality does not stem from differences in the questions posed to or advice received        from the AI, but from how entrepreneurs selected from and implemented the AI advice        they received.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster’s proposition with field-experimental evidence that AI can widen rather than narrow performance differences: stronger entrepreneurs gained while weaker entrepreneurs declined. It also develops the cluster’s conditional account by identifying selection and implementation of advice in open-ended workflows as the mechanism, rather than access alone.
qs: Sub-sample analyses show high performers benefited by just over 15% from the AI        assistant, whereas low performers did about 8% worse.

This increase in performance        inequality does not stem from differences in the questions posed to or advice received        from the AI, but from how entrepreneurs selected from and implemented the AI advice        they received.

st.t: Skill gaps: Assisted equality can hide learning divides
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s task-dependent account by showing that, in a discretionary entrepreneurial setting, an overall null can mask worse point estimates for low performers and better ones for high performers. It also identifies discretion over AI use as an exploratory—not established—explanation. It does not directly assess durable or unassisted skill formation.
qs: Table A12 shows that our negative point estimate among low performers is equivalent to an approximately 8% drop in profits or revenue among low performers, while our positive point estimate among high performers is equivalent to an approximately 15% increase in profits or revenue.
In contrast, the entrepreneurs in our experiment had much more discretion over whether and how they used AI assistance.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The field experiment materially extends the cluster’s proposition beyond constrained tasks: average organisational performance did not improve, effects diverged sharply by initial capability, and successful use depended on users selecting and adapting advice in an open-ended setting. This strengthens the case for selective deployment, user expertise and real-world evaluation rather than inferring value from task-level gains.
qs: Despite receiving similar suggestions from the AI, high performers appear better able to work with the AI to select and implement ideas more tailored to their needs, whereas low performers select more generic suggestions like discounting and advertising that tend to harm business performance.

That our treatment effects differ from                                                20 ^Lprior estimates on the impact of AI provides further evidence of the value of measuring the impact of interventions through real-world field experiments, above and beyond measuring the impact of those same interventions in controlled settings (Aral and Walker, 2012).

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s distinction between assisted task performance and broader economic rewards. Its field experiment finds no average improvement in profits or revenue, increased inequality, and heterogeneous effects that largely benefit entrepreneurs already performing better. It also reinforces the cluster’s warning that gains on bounded tasks may not generalise to open-ended business decisions.
qs: Instead, they suggest that using the AI assistant caused both negative and positive treatment effects, with the benefits largely accruing to entrepreneurs who were already performing better.
However, it remains unclear whether the benefits of such AI feedback generalize to the broader set of tasks that firms engage in.

st.t: Business judgment: Local evidence tempers generic AI advice
st.an: The source directly supports human-led, locally grounded testing: the entrepreneur challenges unrepresentative customer feedback, while the advice shifts toward pilot testing, market research, financial analysis and ongoing review. It also treats recommendations as context-dependent possibilities rather than demonstrated productivity gains, leaving implementation to the entrepreneur and team.
qs: As for the customer feedback, sometimes it may not be reliable since some of the clients we      host are passengers on transit so some opinion they may give may not apply to everyday’s      consideration.

The entrepreneur and the AI assistant also discussed the risks associated with implementing new business strategies, with the AI assistant suggesting thorough market research, pilot testing, financial analysis, risk assessment, and regular feedback review.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source accepts that AI assistance has improved speed and quality on specific business-writing tasks, while explicitly cautioning that these results do not establish benefits across the broader range of firm activities. It therefore supports the cluster’s distinction between task-level gains and whole-job or firm-level productivity, but provides no evidence on durable skill growth.
qs: However, it remains unclear whether the benefits of such AI feedback generalize to the broader set of tasks that firms engage in.

kp.k: Randomized experiment tests AI advice in Kenyan businesses
kp.d: The authors study entrepreneurial performance, not legal services. Their experiment involved 640 Kenyan entrepreneurs, with 322 assigned AI access and 318 assigned International Labour Organization business guides. Recruitment began in May 2023; the experiment ran through November 2023, with three pre-treatment survey waves and four post-treatment waves over two months. Randomization was stratified by gender and baseline performance quartile. The estimates concern assignment to AI access relative to guides, rather than compulsory AI use or comparison with human mentorship.
qs: We measure the impact of AI advice on entrepreneurial performance by running a field experiment with 640 Kenyan entrepreneurs running small and medium businesses.
Control. Participants assigned to the control condition received access to widely used business training materials developed for small and medium businesses by the International Labour Organization.

kp.k: Contextual prompting delivers accessible, discretionary business advice
kp.d: The intervention used GPT-4 through WhatsApp, tailored by prompt engineering rather than fine-tuning. It offered three to five actionable suggestions per query and numbered follow-ups for further exploration. Users selected their questions and which suggestions to implement; the assistant did not execute business decisions autonomously. Onboarding included advice to provide context, ask follow-up questions and consider the possibility of incorrect or harmful recommendations.
qs: The AI assistant used the standard GPT-4 corpus and was contextually tailored using prompt engineering alone.
For each query, the AI assistant provided 3 to 5 tailored, actionable, enumerated strategies.
Sometimes, the advice may be incorrect or bad. Make sure to think about the advice before you use it.

kp.k: AI access produced no statistically detectable average improvement
kp.d: The primary outcome combined standardized weekly and monthly revenue and profit measures. The authors used baseline-adjusted regressions, double-LASSO covariate selection and pooled post-treatment observations. With 99% winsorization, the reported average effect was 0.05 standard deviations (p = 0.36; 95% CI [-0.06, 0.16]); the 95%-winsorized estimate was approximately -0.01 standard deviations (p = 0.92). Failure to reject zero is not a finding that every entrepreneur was unaffected. An exploratory equivalence test rejected an average effect at least as large as the 0.26-standard-deviation comparison threshold drawn from Noy and Zhang.
qs: Using the regression specification outlined in our pre-analysis plan, we first estimate a null average treatment effect (ATE) of AI access on business performance (Estimate A in Figure 3).
we are unable to reject the null hypothesis that the generative AI assistant would have no effect on business performance.

kp.k: Baseline performance predicts unequal benefits and harms
kp.d: The pre-registered baseline-performance split revealed a reported 0.27-standard-deviation difference in treatment effects (p = 0.013). Below-median entrepreneurs experienced a -0.09-standard-deviation effect (p = 0.007; 95% CI [-0.15, -0.03]); above-median entrepreneurs had a noisier +0.19-standard-deviation estimate (p = 0.07; reported 95% CI [-0.02, 0.38]). Thus, the high-performer subgroup estimate did not independently meet the conventional 5% significance threshold. Table A12 translates the all-observation index estimates into average equivalents of -7.89% and +15.05%, respectively; these are index-based conversions, not directly estimated percentage changes for each outcome.
qs: Sub-sample analyses show high performers benefited by just over 15% from the AI assistant, whereas low performers did about 8% worse.
Instead, they suggest that using the AI assistant caused both negative and positive treatment effects, with the benefits largely accruing to entrepreneurs who were already performing better.

kp.k: Robustness analyses reinforce heterogeneity, with specification qualifications
kp.d: Covariate-adjusted raw-outcome analyses retain negative low-performer and positive but noisier high-performer estimates across winsorization and panel restrictions. Generic Machine Learning analyses reject no detectable heterogeneity (p < 0.0001), with estimated group effects of -0.269 and +0.347 standard deviations when using the pre-registered heterogeneity variables. These groups are defined by predicted treatment effects, not the original baseline median split. Pre-registered tests found no heterogeneity by gender or prior frequent ChatGPT use. The appendix also reports weaker, statistically insignificant log-like index results; the authors prefer raw outcomes because of transformation sensitivity to zeros and their interest in absolute performance inequality.

kp.k: Question patterns and advice content showed little differentiation
kp.d: Exploratory analyses found no statistically significant baseline-group differences in willingness to ask questions, message counts, follow-ups, question length or broad topics. Reported question participation was 88.2% for low performers and 84.2% for high performers, with 18.6 versus 15.5 messages and 21.5 versus 25.6 suggestions. Random-forest classifiers using text embeddings could not predict baseline performance status from questions or answers above the no-information rate. These tests support the authors' interpretation that observed differences were not primarily attributable to measured engagement or advice-content differences.
qs: To summarize, we find that low and high-performing entrepreneurs are equally willing to seek advice, ask comparable questions, and receive similar advice.
None of these differences are statistically significant.

kp.k: Advice selection and implementation are proposed differentiating mechanisms
kp.d: The authors' exploratory interpretation is that stronger businesses selected more tailored changes, while weaker businesses more often adopted generic discounting or advertising. Low performers assigned AI were 11.8 percentage points more likely to mention discounting or advertising, against a 39% control rate. High performers assigned AI were 10.8 percentage points more likely to describe working with the assistant and used approximately 20% more uncommon words in business-change descriptions. These text measures support a mechanism hypothesis but do not independently randomize advice selection or establish the profitability of each individual suggestion.
qs: Despite receiving similar suggestions from the AI, high performers appear better able to work with the AI to select and implement ideas more tailored to their needs, whereas low performers select more generic suggestions like discounting and advertising that tend to harm business performance.
Relative to the base rate, low performers are 30% more likely to discount products or invest in ads.

kp.k: Text-based mechanism evidence depends on explicit assumptions
kp.d: The authors infer influence of advice content on reported business changes by controlling for question content, arguing that questions are the assistant's only information about entrepreneurs. Their word-level estimate is a 2.84-percentage-point increase in a word appearing in business-change text when it appears in advice; embedding analyses show a similar relationship. They explicitly acknowledge that advice content was not randomized, causal interpretation depends on their model of language generation, bag-of-words assumptions are strong, and keyword measures are imperfect. Mentioning AI or using uncommon words is an operational measure, not a direct assessment of learning or judgment.
qs: While our experiment does not randomize the content of the AI generated advice, the structure of our intervention allows us to estimate the impact of advice on business changes simply by controlling for the content of the messages sent to the AI by the entrepreneur.

kp.k: Open-ended work may amplify the importance of judgment
kp.d: The authors contrast their results with cited experiments in writing, coding, consulting and customer support that generally found gains concentrated among weaker performers. Their proposed explanation is task discretion: entrepreneurs choose problems, receive varied recommendations and must select among potentially beneficial and detrimental actions. This is a framework derived from the entrepreneurial setting, not direct evidence about lawyers, legal staffing or legal-service productivity. Figure 6 illustrates the proposed mechanism rather than measuring a distribution of individual advice returns.
qs: A major difference between our field experiment and prior research on the economic impacts of generative AI is the level of discretion participants were granted in how and when they used AI assistance.
In our experiment, participants have discretion over which questions they ask and which advice they choose to implement.
High performers appear better at selecting advice and implementing tasks that can benefit their specific business needs.

kp.k: Low delivery costs create conditional mentorship opportunities
kp.d: The authors position generative AI as a potentially scalable source of personalized feedback in developing economies. They compare high-performer point estimates with the 10%–15% improvements associated with human training programs and report assistant costs of a few dollars per participant versus hundreds for many training programs. This is a comparison with external research, not a randomized demonstration that AI matches human mentors or is universally cost-effective; harms among weaker businesses qualify the opportunity.
qs: our AI assistant costs a few dollars per participant whereas most training programs cost hundreds of dollars (USD) per participant
That being said, we also find evidence that generative AI can widen the gap between low- and high-performing businesses in these contexts.

kp.k: Sample, duration and adoption context limit generalization
kp.d: The online-recruited sample was young and highly educated: median age 26, 53% completed college, 32% were women and 64% of businesses had no employees. Follow-up was strong, with 634 participants completing at least one post-treatment survey and 622 all four, but outcomes were survey-based and post-treatment observation lasted only two months. The authors consider within-sample competitive spillovers unlikely because of geographic and sector dispersion; they do not establish economy-wide effects or rule out spillovers involving outside competitors. Results may change with longer exposure or broader AI adoption.
qs: A majority of these businesses (64%) operated without any employees.
It is possible that performance spillovers occur between entrepreneurs in our sample and their competitors that are not in our sample.
If there were a greater level of overall generative AI saturation in Kenya, our results may not hold.

kp.k: Improved training and system design remain untested possibilities
kp.d: The authors suggest that fine-tuning, revised prompts and additional user training could strengthen benefits and reduce harms, but do not test these remedies. They identify unresolved questions about why some users persist despite negative returns, whether poor advice selection can improve, whether deeper capability differences or training-data biases explain heterogeneity, and how AI affects entrepreneurial learning. The assistant itself did not learn during the experiment. Their recommendation is further real-world experimentation rather than assuming that more capable models or broader deployment will automatically improve outcomes.
qs: while we find that low-performing entrepreneurs implement advice that harms performance, we do not know if we can improve their choices or if the negative effects stem from more fundamental differences in skills or capabilities.
Finally, the AI assistant in our experiment does not learn, nor have we explored how the AI assistant impacted entrepreneurial learning.
As our findings show, generative AI is already capable of impacting real, open-ended, and unstructured economic outcomes, though in uneven and unexpected ways.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Otis, Clarke, Delecourt, Holtz and Koning claim that AI business advice can change real entrepreneurial outcomes while widening differences between initially stronger and weaker businesses.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain source about Kenyan entrepreneurship, not legal services. The authors do not detect a statistically significant average effect of access to their GPT-4 assistant. They report a treatment-effect difference of approximately 0.27 standard deviations between above- and below-median baseline performers. Their headline percentage equivalents are approximately a 15% improvement for high performers and an 8% decline for low performers. They interpret exploratory evidence as suggesting that selection and implementation of advice, rather than differences in questions or suggestions received, explain the divergence: stronger performers identify tailored improvements, while weaker performers more often adopt generic discounting and advertising strategies. They also suggest AI could provide personalized mentorship at substantially lower cost than human training, without claiming universal benefits.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The outcome claims rest on a randomized field experiment; the proposed mechanism rests on exploratory text analyses and participant accounts.
pts.d: The experiment assigned 640 Kenyan entrepreneurs to free WhatsApp-based GPT-4 assistance or International Labour Organization business guides, stratifying assignment by gender and baseline performance. Outcomes combined self-reported weekly and monthly profits and revenue, measured across three baseline and four post-treatment surveys. The analysis used baseline adjustment, double-LASSO covariate selection and entrepreneur-clustered standard errors; 622 participants completed all four follow-ups. The reported low-performer estimate was -0.09 standard deviations (p = 0.007), while the high-performer estimate was +0.19 (p = 0.07), making the latter less precisely estimated and not significant at the conventional 5% threshold. Percentage figures are conversions from the performance-index estimates, not separately estimated uniform percentage gains in each outcome. Robustness analyses include alternative winsorization, difference-in-differences and Generic ML heterogeneity tests. The supplied text reports p = 0.013 for the 0.27-standard-deviation interaction but prints a confidence interval crossing zero; Table A4 reports an interaction of 0.267 with standard error 0.107. Mechanism evidence includes chat logs, topic classification, embeddings, keyword matching and accounts of business changes. These analyses were not preregistered and did not randomize which advice participants implemented. Low performers were 11.8 percentage points more likely to mention discounting or advertising; high performers used approximately 20% more uncommon words, interpreted as greater specificity. Cost comparisons draw on the assistant's reported delivery cost and published human-training studies, rather than a direct randomized comparison against human mentors.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The findings concern short-run access to a particular GPT-4 assistant in 2023; longer-run effects and improved deployment designs remain open questions.
pts.d: Recruitment and fieldwork ran from May to November 2023; the authors describe three months of baseline measurement and two months of post-treatment observation. The assistant used standard GPT-4 with a context-specific system prompt, brief onboarding, free unlimited access and reminders. It supplied suggestions but left entrepreneurs responsible for deciding whether, when and how to implement them. The authors contrast this discretionary, open-ended setting with earlier studies assigning narrower tasks. They suggest, rather than establish, that fine-tuning, improved prompts or additional user training might increase gains and reduce harms. They explicitly leave uncertain whether weaker performers can be taught to select better advice, whether different training data would help, and how experience, learning and widespread adoption would change outcomes. Market-wide effects could include stronger price competition or beneficial diffusion of practices; the experiment does not establish either.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied beneficiaries and adversely affected users are Kenyan small-business owners differentiated by initial business performance.
pts.d: Participants operated businesses across 44 Kenyan counties, including food, clothing, agriculture and information-technology services. They were relatively young and educated: average age was approximately 26, 53% had completed college, 32% were women and 64% operated without employees. High and low performance refer to the baseline revenue-and-profit index, not independently measured expertise or AI skill. Above-median businesses had positive estimated returns; below-median businesses experienced negative estimated returns. The preregistered analyses did not detect heterogeneity by gender or prior weekly ChatGPT use. The authors extend the potential relevance to entrepreneurs and firms in low- and middle-income countries, and to managers and policymakers considering affordable mentorship. These broader applications are possibilities, not direct experimental findings for every population. The source makes no empirical claim about lawyers, law firms, legal employment or access to justice.
